old.headline: The Achilles signal from Thursday is the whole story this week — we pull quality out, keep running only if pain stays low and not worsening, and you get it looked at by a sports physio.
old.analysis:
## Why this shape

You stopped Thursday's session because the Achilles got sharper with pace, and Saturday it was stiff for a mile before settling. That is the classic early-warning pattern and the right response is a short, soft week — not a lost block. The race is nine weeks out and your aerobic base is in good shape, so losing a sharpening week costs you nothing.

Quality is out this week. Pace changes and push-off load the Achilles the most, and that is exactly what provoked it. We hold easy aerobic running at flat routes only, and skip the Thursday hill loop.

## How to run this week

Use a simple traffic-light rule each day. Pain under 2/10 that eases in the first mile and does not get worse while running: go. Pain 3/10 or climbing during the run: stop and walk home. Any sharp pain, swelling, or morning limp: do not run and get it looked at.

Shoes stay in the Ghost 16 all week — more stack, less heel drop stress than the Speed 4. Skip calf raises and anything that loads the Achilles hard until a professional clears you. Short, gentle walking is fine and helpful.

## What's next

If the Achilles settles cleanly by Sunday, next week we rebuild to a normal easy week and then layer quality back in the week after. If it is still grumbling, we hold easy or cross-train longer. Nine weeks is enough runway to protect this and still run 3:30 — pushing through it now is what turns a tight tendon into a six-week problem.

answers.question: Should I stop running for a few days, or keep going with easy runs?
answers.answer:
Easy running is okay this week **only** if the Achilles behaves. Use this rule each run:

| Pain during run | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Under 2/10, eases after first mile | Continue as planned |
| 3/10 or climbing | Stop and walk home |
| Sharp, or morning limp next day | Do not run, rest and get it assessed |

I would also take Thursday as a second rest day this week to give it an extra 48-hour window. No pace changes, no hills, no strides. Short walks and gentle ankle mobility are fine. If two consecutive runs feel clean, we are on track to rebuild next week.

answers.question: How do I know if this is serious?
answers.answer:
That is a question for a sports physio, not me — and I would book one this week rather than wait. I can't diagnose anything, but the pattern coaches watch for is: pain that sharpens with pace, morning stiffness that takes more than a few steps to clear, visible swelling or a lump on the tendon, pain when you press it, or pain going up stairs or doing a single-leg calf raise. Any of those earn a visit.

The reassuring signs are: tightness that eases within the first mile of easy running, no morning limp, no swelling, and settles with a day or two off. You are in a mixed picture right now, which is why we train conservatively and get professional eyes on it.

safetyCallouts.title: Get the Achilles assessed this week
safetyCallouts.body:
Pain that sharpens with pace and lingers as morning stiffness is worth a professional look, not a wait-and-see. Please book a sports physio or sports medicine doctor in the next few days — they can tell you what's going on and what loading is safe.

Stop running and seek same-day care if you get sudden sharp pain, a pop or snap sensation, visible swelling, or you can't push off the foot normally. I'm coaching the training around this; the medical read needs to come from a qualified professional.

answers.answer:
**1. Stop for a few days, or keep easy miles going?**

My honest take: take Mon and Tue fully off running, swap in a brisk walk or easy bike if you want to move. If on Wed morning the Achilles is quiet getting out of bed (no limp, no sharp pinch, stiffness gone within a couple of steps), try a short easy run and see how the next 24 hours feel. If it stays quiet, build back through the week as planned. If it flares, stop and book the physio sooner.

The reason to pause rather than push is that the pattern — tight by mile 2, sharper with speed, lingering stiffness after — is the kind of thing that quietens quickly with a few days of load reduction and gets stubborn if you train through it. A short, early pullback almost never costs a marathon. Training through does.

**2. How do I know if this is serious?**

I'm a coach, not a clinician, so the real answer is: a sports physio can tell you in one visit, and I'd book that this week regardless. Please don't wait on this one.

From a coaching lens, the signals that mean stop running and get seen now:

- Sharp or pinching pain in the tendon, not just tightness
- A visible or palpable lump, thickening, or swelling
- Morning stiffness that takes more than a few minutes of walking to clear
- Any limping, or pain going up or down stairs
- Pain that gets worse run-to-run instead of better

Signals that usually settle with a few easy days and good calf care: mild stiffness in the first mile that eases, no pain at easy pace, nothing lingering the next morning. Either way, the physio visit is the right move — it turns guesswork into a plan.

new.analysis:
## Why this week looks nothing like the plan I'd have written a week ago

Thursday's session told us something important: the tendon didn't like the pace change, and it's still talking after Sunday. I'd rather give up one quality week now than lose four to a cranky Achilles in October. With 9 weeks to race day, the fitness you've built — 44 miles with a 16-miler, marathon pace felt controlled — is banked. It doesn't disappear in a quiet week.

## What I'm doing with the shape

All running is easy and shorter than last week, with a planned mid-week check-in with yourself before Wednesday's run. Tuesday is optional — if the tendon is anything more than mildly stiff on waking, make it a walk or bike and shift the easy miles later. Thursday becomes an easy aerobic run instead of a workout; we're not touching 8:00/mi until the physio clears you and three consecutive runs feel clean.

## The long run

I've held Sunday at 10 miles rather than pushing to 14 – 16. Time on feet without any pace stress is the right dose this week. If anything twinges in the first three miles, turn around — no heroics. If it's clean through 10, we can step back into a normal build next week.

## What I'll do with next week

If this week lands quiet and the physio is reassuring, we rebuild toward 38 – 40 miles with a modest quality session (likely short MP reps in flats, not the Endorphin Speed) and a 14-mile long run. If symptoms persist, we hold flat again and I'll lean more on cross-training to protect the aerobic base. Either path keeps Lakeshore 3:30 realistic — training through this does not.

safetyCallouts.title: Book a sports physio this week.
safetyCallouts.body: The Achilles got sharp enough to stop a session and is still stiff two days later. A physio can assess the tendon properly and give you a clear return-to-running plan — that's outside what I can do as a coach. Until then, no speed work, no hills, and stop any run that gets painful rather than just stiff.

safetyCallouts.title: Red-flag symptoms to act on.
safetyCallouts.body: If you get a visible lump on the tendon, swelling, a popping or snapping sensation, sudden weakness pushing off, or pain that makes you limp, stop running and get seen urgently rather than waiting on the regular appointment.
